title: Course method: from an urgent outcome to a small paid course selling on the brand's own site
ends_with: The owner holds a live course on the brand's learn site with every lesson video, caption file, transcript, worksheet and deliverable in the course folder, a Stripe checkout with its order bump, the welcome emails loaded, a paste-ready upload kit and the live link, all linked on the job in HQ.

outside_hq.what: Point the brand's learn address (for example learn.allmightysupreme.com) at the course engine.
outside_hq.why: The address did not resolve when checked on November 12, 2026; only he can change his domain's settings.
outside_hq.how_owner_does_it: Open the domain's DNS settings at the registrar, add the record Lovable shows under the engine's Domains setting, tap Save. Skip if the address already opens.

outside_hq.what: Connect Stripe to the course engine once.
outside_hq.why: Lovable needs the Stripe key entered in its editor by the account owner.
outside_hq.how_owner_does_it: Open the engine in Lovable, connect Stripe when prompted, paste the key from the Stripe Dashboard under Developers, API keys. Skip if already connected.

outside_hq.what: Create the brand's YouTube channel if it has none, for unlisted lesson videos.
outside_hq.why: Only he can create a Google account channel.
outside_hq.how_owner_does_it: In the YouTube app, tap your picture, Create a channel, use the brand name. Skip if it exists.

outside_hq.what: Make the one real test purchase in stage 10.
outside_hq.why: A real card is the only proof the checkout works.
outside_hq.how_owner_does_it: Follow the stage 10 card on your phone.

stages.title: Find the urgent outcome people already search for
stages.what: Claude finds what buyers in this niche are searching for and complaining about right now, then turns it into three candidate course outcomes, each one finished result a buyer can reach in one sitting or one week.
stages.why: His rule is one specific outcome that people will pay for now because the pain is urgent, and research before building. Buyers ask for refunds when the course promises more than it delivers or they get stuck without an early win, so the outcome has to be small, concrete and wanted.
inputs: his topic idea, if he has one
the brand's Answer Bank and idea evidence in HQ
existing course and product rows for the brand

decided.value: Google and YouTube search suggestions, Reddit questions sorted Top and All Time then checked for the past year, the 1 to 3 star reviews of the best-selling books, courses and guides on the same problem, and the brand's own outliers
decided.reason: His review-mining protocol and Signal Engine; free routes first.

decided.value: A result the buyer can check they have, written as: When you're done, you'll have ___. If the blank cannot be filled with something concrete, it is a free post, not a paid course
decided.reason: His Action Labs finish-line rule.

decided.value: Reachable in 45 to 90 minutes of doing, or one short week
decided.reason: His Action Labs format; mini courses that try to squeeze in a full course fail.

decided.value: Every app or AI feature the outcome depends on is checked on its maker's help page this week, with the date written down
decided.reason: Apps change under courses; for example custom GPTs retire on December 11, 2026, so a course built on them would break.

decided.what: Whether a weak score stops his idea
decided.value: No. The score ranks and sharpens the brief; it never blocks a topic he picked
decided.reason: His November 13, 2026 override.

work: Load the brand kit from HQ and the brand's existing course rows (channel_products and action_items that mention course) so nothing is duplicated.
Pull Google and YouTube search suggestions for the topic's main phrases and their how-to, for-free, for-beginners and with-a-named-tool variants; save the raw lists with the date.

Read the top questions on the topic's subreddits (Top, All Time, then past year) and the 1 to 3 star reviews on the best-selling books and courses for the same problem; cluster complaints and quote each at ten words or fewer with its link.
List the competing paid courses and guides you can see (title, price, promised result, length) and what their buyers praise.
Check every app, plan limit and feature the outcome needs on the maker's own help page and record the date.
Write three candidate outcomes, each with its finish-line sentence, the buyer, the urgent pain in the buyer's words, the evidence links and the time to finish.
File the complaints in the Answer Bank and update the idea score and evidence on the course row in HQ.

output.name: Demand sheet: search suggestions, questions, complaint clusters, competitor table
output.lands_in: the course folder in Google Drive under Supreme Team HQ - Brands, brand folder, Courses, course title, linked on the job in HQ

output.name: Three candidate outcomes with finish-line sentences and evidence
output.lands_in: the job in HQ and the course row's idea evidence

stages.check: Three outcomes exist, each with a finish-line sentence, at least three linked pieces of demand evidence and a dated check of every tool it depends on.
checks: At least five complaint clusters are filed with short quotes and links.
No outcome depends on a feature its maker has announced will retire.
stages.if_fail: Widen to the neighbouring search phrases and the next ten competitors, or narrow the buyer (for example beginners, small business owners, people over 50) and repeat.

stages.title: Approve the one-screen course brief
stages.what: Claude fills a one-screen brief: the buyer, the one outcome, the finish-line sentence, the complaints it fixes, the mission map, the price ladder, where it sells and the refund line. The owner picks the title, the price ladder and where it sells, then approves.
stages.why: No brief, no build. Settling the outcome, price and host here prevents the costly late changes: a sales page that promises more than the lessons deliver, or a checkout rebuilt on a second platform.
inputs: three candidate outcomes and the demand sheet
the brand kit and its offer ladder
the state of the brand's course engine, checkout and email sender

choices.question: Which outcome and title should this course be?
choices.help: Each option is one finished result. The title says the result and the time it takes.
choices.generate_from: The three outcomes from stage 1, each written as a title of 12 words or fewer naming the result and the time, plus its finish-line sentence and its strongest piece of evidence.

options.label: Generated outcome 1
options.pick_when: It has the most search and complaint evidence and the smallest finish line.

options.label: Generated outcome 2
options.pick_when: You know this one best from your own work.

options.label: Generated outcome 3
options.pick_when: It leads most naturally into the brand's next paid step.

choices.question: How should it be priced?
choices.help: The order bump is a small add-on ticked on the checkout page. The next step is offered on the finish screen and in email after the buyer finishes.

options.label: $27 course, $17 order bump, $97 next step
options.pick_when: It is the brand's first course or it has no reviews yet. This is your November 10 plan and it matches the $17 to $27 bump pattern in 2026 upsell data.

options.label: $47 course, no order bump
options.pick_when: The outcome is bigger (a full kit or several finished pieces) and you want one simple price.

options.label: $27 founding price, rising to $47 after 10 reviews
options.pick_when: You want the review-first launch but expect the course to hold a higher price later.

choices.question: Where should it sell and play?
choices.help: The host is where the buyer pays and watches. Your own site keeps the sale and the customer list; a marketplace may bring buyers but takes more and owns the relationship.

options.label: Your own course engine at the brand's learn address (for example learn.allmightysupreme.com) with Stripe checkout
options.pick_when: Default. The engine is already built, Stripe is live, you keep about $25.92 of a $27 sale and own the list. This is your November 10 decision.

options.label: Payhip course page
options.pick_when: The brand's engine checkout is not built yet and you want it selling this week; 5 percent fee, Payhip handles EU and UK VAT.

options.label: Whop
options.pick_when: You want a marketplace and affiliates to sell it; read Whop's current platform fee first, because its fee page lists only processing.

choices.question: Is the brief right?
choices.help: Read the one screen. Approving starts the interview; nothing is written before this.

options.label: Approve
options.pick_when: The buyer, the outcome and the missions sound right.

options.label: Change something (say it by voice)
options.pick_when: The buyer, the promise or a mission is off.

decided.value: An Action Lab: 3 to 5 missions of 10 to 25 minutes each, 45 to 90 minutes in total, ending in one finished deliverable the buyer downloads
decided.reason: His Action Labs format; short mini courses of 3 to 5 lessons are the 2026 practitioner pattern.

decided.value: 14-day money-back on request, stated on the sales page, the checkout and the receipt
decided.reason: Matches Teachable's standard 14-day window and keeps trust high for a new brand with no reviews. EU buyers lose the 14-day withdrawal right only if they expressly agree to start right away, so the checkout carries that tick box.

decided.value: No earnings, income or results promises; examples are labeled as examples; money courses show what the buyer will make (an offer, a plan), never what they will earn
decided.reason: FTC money-making notice and Operation AI Comply; Stripe prohibits get-rich-quick offers.

decided.value: The course opens for sale only after it is built and produced; no presell
decided.reason: His November 12, 2026 decision.

decided.value: The brief names which existing course this one joins or replaces so each brand always has one live
decided.reason: His November 10, 2026 decision.

work: Fill the brief: buyer, outcome, finish-line sentence, complaints it fixes with links, what five-star buyers praise, mission map with minutes, deliverable, price ladder, host, refund line, next step, launch week.
Check the title against the brand's banned words and against existing course and book titles for confusion.
Write the gap questions for the stage 3 interview.
Register or update the course row on HQ's Products page (channel_products) at status brief, then approved.

output.name: Approved course brief
output.format: one screen in the job plus brief.md
output.lands_in: the course folder, linked on the job in HQ

stages.check: The owner tapped Approve, and the brief names the buyer, the finish-line sentence, the mission map, the price ladder, the host and the refund line.
checks: The finish-line sentence names something the buyer can hold or open.
The total minutes are between 45 and 90.
stages.if_fail: Claude rewrites the brief from his voice note and shows it again.

skip.rule: The recommended option is used for every choice and the brief is approved as written.

stages.title: Answer the teaching interview by voice
stages.what: The owner answers six to eight questions by voice about how he actually does this, what beginners get wrong and what he would tell a friend. His words become the parts of the lessons nobody else can copy.
stages.why: Teaching is the work he likes most, and his own method is the difference between this course and free answers. Udemy, for example, refuses fully AI-generated courses with minimal instructor input, which shows where the market draws the line.
inputs: approved brief and its gap questions
his existing posts, threads, Drive documents and saved courses on the topic

choices.question: When do you want to answer?
choices.help: About 20 minutes by voice. Half sentences are fine. Every question has skip, don't know, and give me an example.

options.label: Now, by voice
options.pick_when: You have 20 minutes, for example parked between deliveries.

options.label: In two short sessions today
options.pick_when: You only have ten-minute gaps.

options.label: Skip, use what I have already said
options.pick_when: You are slammed this week and you have posted about this topic before.

choices.question: Answer this question in your own words.
choices.help: One question at a time. Say skip at any point.
choices.generate_from: The gap questions from the brief, drawn from the kdp-book interview in knowledge mode: how you do it, the order you do it in, what beginners get wrong, what you got wrong, the one thing to remember, a real moment it worked.

decided.value: Claude uses only his existing material, quoted with its source, and marks each lesson that has no item from him; the course still moves and the quality card shows the gap
decided.reason: Nothing is invented; scores advise and never block.

decided.value: Never required. His voice answers are notes, not lesson audio. Using his own voice or face in lessons is an optional later upgrade
decided.reason: His standing rule: no filming or recording to make content.

work: Pull his existing words on the topic first, with sources.
Ask only the gaps, one question at a time, following the kdp-book interview rules.
Save his answers unedited, tagged by mission.
Flag every number, health, money or legal statement for stage 6.
stages.check: Every mission has at least one item from his words or existing material, or a marked gap listed for stage 7.
checks: No answer was rewritten before saving.
stages.if_fail: One follow-up question per empty mission, or record the gap.

skip.rule: Claude uses only what the owner has already said in posts, threads and documents, quoted with its source, and leaves a marker where a story would help.

stages.title: Design the missions and the finished result
stages.what: Claude designs the course backwards from the finished deliverable: the missions, the lessons inside each, the do-this-today assignment and worksheet for each, the I'm stuck hint, the worked example, the one AI step and the deliverable template.
stages.why: Completion is what turns buyers into reviews. In Ruzuku's 2026 data, students who finished a lesson in their first week completed at 78 percent against 17 percent for those who did not, and courses with assessments completed at 59 percent against 42 percent.

decided.value: 3 to 5 missions; each mission is 1 to 3 short lessons, an assignment done inside the mission, and a saved answer that feeds the deliverable
decided.reason: His Action Labs format; Kajabi's 2026 guidance is to end every module with an action step and cut anything outside the promised result.

decided.value: Under 6 minutes per lesson video
decided.reason: In 6.9 million edX sessions, median engagement was at most 6 minutes whatever the video length.

decided.value: Mission 1 finishes in 15 minutes or less and produces something real
decided.reason: First-week activity is the strongest completion signal in the 2026 data.

decided.value: One three-question check per mission, answers explained
decided.reason: Courses with assessments completed more often.

decided.value: At most one AI button, where it does the heavy lifting, with a per-student use limit and a paste-ready backup prompt
decided.reason: AI calls in a published Lovable app use run credits; the free monthly AI grant is 4 credits.

decided.value: Every software step carries the app name, plan and the date it was checked
decided.reason: His acceptance test for AI and small business products.

work: Write the deliverable template first: the sections the buyer will download at the end.
Map each section to a mission and each mission to its steps (short answer, long answer, choice, number, calculator, built sentence, AI draft, list), the way the engine stores them.
Write each mission's I'm stuck hint and one worked example per step.
Write the claims table: every number, rule or product claim with its source.
List the lesson titles, one job each, with minutes.

output.name: Mission map, step list, deliverable template, claims table
output.lands_in: the course folder, linked on the job in HQ

stages.check: Every mission ends in a saved answer that appears in the deliverable, mission 1 is 15 minutes or less, and every claim has a source or a flag.
checks: No lesson is planned over 6 minutes of video.
Total minutes are within the brief's range.
stages.if_fail: Cut content that does not feed the deliverable, then re-time.

stages.title: Write the lessons, worksheets and scripts
stages.what: Claude writes every lesson as a short script with its on-screen slide or walkthrough notes, the written lesson text for people who prefer reading, the worksheet and assignment for each mission, and the hints and worked examples.
stages.why: Filler and missing steps are the most repeated course complaints. One voice, one source of truth per lesson and nothing invented keep the course short and trustworthy.

decided.value: The brand kit's voice; for Allmighty Supreme his plain professional-casual register, no em dashes, no urban vernacular
decided.reason: His brand rules.

decided.value: About 150 words per minute, so a 6-minute lesson is about 900 words
decided.reason: Average speaking rate in the edX study was 156 words per minute, and faster delivery held attention.

decided.value: Hook (the problem in the buyer's words), the one move, a shown example, the do-this-now step, the bridge to the next lesson
decided.reason: Kdp-book chapter anatomy adapted to a lesson.

decided.value: Every item from his words is tagged OWNER in the draft and removed at file time
decided.reason: So he can confirm each is real in stage 7.

work: Draft one lesson at a time in one thread, against the brief, the interview and the claims table.
Write slide notes or a step-by-step screen walkthrough for each lesson, with exact menu and button names from the dated tool check.
Write each mission's worksheet with one instruction line and one filled example row.
Write the engine step text: title, body, hint, worked example, choices.
Write the deliverable's export text.

output.name: Lesson scripts, written lessons, worksheets, step text
output.lands_in: the course folder, linked on the job in HQ

stages.check: Every lesson script is 900 words or fewer, every worksheet has an instruction line and a filled example, and every software step names its date checked.
checks: Every mission carries an OWNER item or a listed gap.
stages.if_fail: Cut the long lesson and redraft it; never patch.

stages.title: Run the quality gates and a cold test run
stages.what: Claude runs the writing gates, then a fresh agent takes the whole course as a beginner on the real apps and must finish the deliverable. Then the claims and compliance pass.
stages.why: Buyers punish courses that do not produce the promised result. A cold run on the live apps catches changed menus and missing steps before buyers do, and the compliance pass keeps money and results claims inside FTC and Stripe rules.

decided.value: Sweep, swap test, specificity floor, repetition, worksheet test, cold read, critic pass by ChatGPT with the three-star prompt, final five
decided.reason: His kdp-book gates, applied to lessons.

decided.value: A fresh agent with no context follows the course on the current apps, timed, and must produce the deliverable; every place it got stuck is fixed
decided.reason: His acceptance test: test the workflow the checklist claims to support.

decided.value: No earnings figures, no typical-results claims without proof, no risk-free, no act now, no no-experience-needed promises
decided.reason: These are the practices listed in the FTC money-making notice; the FTC's 2024 AI cases targeted exactly these promises.

decided.value: One plain line on the sales page and the welcome screen: lessons are produced with AI voice and visuals from the author's own method
decided.reason: Honest framing; Udemy requires AI-use disclosure in the course description if the course ever goes there.

work: Run the sweep script and gates 2 to 8 on each mission.
Run the cold test run and log time per mission and every stuck point.
Update the claims table to verified, qualified, uncertain or contradicted; cut uncertain claims.
Check the title and copy for trademarks and earnings language.
Write the quality card: advisory score, gate results, cold-run time, open flags.
stages.check: The cold-run agent finished the deliverable within the brief's minutes, and no claim is uncertain or contradicted in the text.
checks: No sentence promises income or a specific result.
Every software step matches the app as it is today.
stages.if_fail: Failing lessons go back to stage 5; a step that no longer works goes back to stage 4.

stages.title: Pick the lesson style and approve one sample lesson
stages.what: Claude produces mission 1's first lesson in the recommended style. The owner watches it on his phone, picks the style and voice, confirms the OWNER items are true and approves.
stages.why: Only he can judge his brand's look and voice and confirm his own stories. Approving one lesson before producing all of them keeps the credits spent only once.
inputs: list of OWNER items and gaps

choices.question: How should the lessons look?
choices.help: All four are made with AI. None needs you on camera.

options.label: AI voice over clean slides and on-screen steps
options.pick_when: Default. Best for teaching a process; cheapest to update when an app changes.

options.label: AI voice over a built screen walkthrough
options.pick_when: The course is about using an app, and seeing each click matters.

options.label: AI presenter (your AI clone when ready, or a stock presenter)
options.pick_when: The brand sells on a face and the presenter is labeled as AI.

options.label: Written lessons with images, no video
options.pick_when: The buyer mostly reads, or you want zero voice credits.

choices.question: Which voice reads the lessons?
choices.generate_from: Two or three ElevenLabs voices that fit the brand kit's voice notes, each reading the same 20 seconds of the sample.

options.label: Generated voice 1
options.pick_when: It sounds most like the brand.

options.label: Generated voice 2
options.pick_when: You want a calmer read.

options.label: Your AI clone voice
options.pick_when: It is ready and you want the course in your voice.

choices.question: Produce all lessons with ElevenLabs on your plan?
choices.help: About 1,000 ElevenLabs credits per minute of narration, so a 25-minute course uses about 25,000 credits of your monthly allowance. This spends credits, so it needs your yes.

options.label: Yes, produce all lessons (his go required)
options.pick_when: The sample sounds right.

options.label: No, keep it text and slides only
options.pick_when: You want no credits spent on this course.

choices.question: Is the sample lesson right?
choices.help: Watch it on your phone, tap any OWNER item that is wrong, say comments by voice.

options.label: Approve
options.pick_when: It looks and sounds like the brand and the OWNER items are true.

options.label: Change something (say it by voice)
options.pick_when: Something about the look, voice or a claim is off.

decided.value: Claude uses voice over slides with voice 1, keeps only OWNER items with a quoted source, and produces the text-only version until he says yes to credits
decided.reason: Nothing waits forever; no credits without his yes.

decided.value: Natural voice at about 150 words a minute with pauses edited out, one idea per slide, real screens instead of stock where a tool is taught, captions on, no AI tells in the script
decided.reason: Low-quality AI visuals and audio are what Udemy removes; the edX study found tighter, enthusiastic delivery held attention.

work: Produce lesson 1 in the recommended style with two or three voice options.
Show it in the job with the OWNER list.
Record his picks and comments in the brief.
stages.check: He picked a style and a voice and tapped Approve, or the skip defaults were applied.
checks: Every OWNER item is confirmed or removed.
stages.if_fail: Claude remakes the sample from his comments.

skip.rule: The recommended lesson style and voice are used and the sample lesson is approved as made.

stages.title: Produce the lesson videos, captions and downloads
stages.what: Claude produces every lesson in the approved style: narration with ElevenLabs, slides and screen walkthroughs rendered with HyperFrames, captions and transcripts from the scripts, and the worksheets and deliverable as PDFs.
stages.why: Captions and transcripts are the accessibility baseline (WCAG level A) and help buyers who watch on a phone with the sound off. Building visuals from code keeps every lesson editable when an app changes.

decided.value: A caption file for every video, written from the script so it is exact, with speaker and meaningful sounds noted
decided.reason: WCAG 1.2.2 captions are level A; YouTube's automatic captions vary in quality.

decided.value: A full text version of each lesson, including what the screen shows
decided.reason: WCAG 1.2.3 accepts a full text alternative.

decided.value: HyperFrames renders HTML compositions to MP4 locally, free, Apache 2.0 license
decided.reason: No per-render fees.

decided.value: Videos uploaded to YouTube as unlisted and embedded in the engine
decided.reason: The engine is built for unlisted YouTube embeds so hosting costs nothing; unlisted means anyone with the link can watch, which is acceptable at this price.

decided.value: Worksheets and deliverable template as PDF in Letter size, readable on a phone, 12 point body or larger
decided.reason: His shelf rules for downloads.

work: Generate narration per lesson after his credits yes; trim pauses.
Build each lesson's slides or walkthrough as a HyperFrames composition and render to MP4.
Write VTT caption files from the scripts, timed to the audio.
Build worksheet and deliverable PDFs with ReportLab and look at every page as an image.
Upload videos to the brand's YouTube channel as unlisted with captions attached and record each link.

output.name: Lesson videos, captions, transcripts, PDFs
output.lands_in: the course folder (media and files subfolders)

stages.check: Every lesson has a video (or approved text-only page), a caption file, a transcript and a working unlisted link; every PDF opens on a phone with nothing cut off.
checks: Captions match the narration word for word.
stages.if_fail: Re-render the failing lesson; if narration is wrong, fix the script and regenerate only that lesson.

stages.title: Build the sales page, checkout, order bump and emails
stages.what: Claude writes the sales page, sets up the course, order bump and next-step products in Stripe, writes the welcome and nudge emails, and builds the course into the engine as a draft.
stages.why: Warm traffic from his posts wants confirmation, not discovery. The order bump is where low-priced offers make their margin: 2026 upsell data puts order bumps at about 38 percent acceptance, though no public benchmark exists for course sales pages themselves.

choices.question: The brand's engine has no checkout yet. How should it be built? (first course on a brand only)
choices.help: Skip this if the engine already takes payments.

options.label: Claude builds it through GitHub, no credits
options.pick_when: The engine's code is linked to GitHub.

options.label: One Lovable build, estimated 10 to 20 credits (his go required)
options.pick_when: GitHub is not linked or the build is large. Estimate based on the engine's first build at 20 credits.

decided.value: Headline with the result and time, who it is for, the finish-line sentence, what you will have (with a picture of the deliverable), the missions with minutes, a sample lesson, who it is not for, price, refund line, FAQ, the AI-production line
decided.reason: His warm-traffic product page rules; overpromising drives refunds.

decided.value: One related add-on at $7 to $17 in Stripe Checkout's Cross-sells to field; quantity is always 1
decided.reason: Stripe cross-sells need a product with exactly one active price in the same currency.

decided.value: Offered on the engine's finish screen and in email 3, never before the buyer finishes
decided.reason: His Action Labs completion screen and next-step fields.

decided.value: Access is granted from the checkout.session.completed webhook, works if called twice, and the success page shows access immediately
decided.reason: His own-site delivery method.

decided.value: Receipt and sign-in from the engine; email 1 at purchase (start mission 1 tonight), email 2 at day 2 only if mission 1 is unfinished, email 3 on finishing (the next step), email 4 at day 7 asking for a review
decided.reason: First-week activity predicts completion.

decided.value: HQ's own email sequences once that part of the sales system is built. Until then the four emails are saved in HQ, and the course engine sends the receipt and the sign-in.
decided.reason: You decided on November 27, 2026 to cancel GoHighLevel.

decided.value: Turn on Stripe Tax before selling to places where the brand is registered, or sell through Payhip
decided.reason: Stripe Tax costs 0.5 percent per transaction where registered; Payhip collects EU and UK VAT.

work: Write the sales page and the checkout text, including the refund line and the EU immediate-access tick box wording.
Create the Stripe products: the course at the brief's price, the order bump, the next step; set the cross-sell on the course product.
Load the course into the engine as a draft: lab, missions, steps, videos, hints, worked examples, deliverable template, AI step and its use limit, next-step fields.
Write the four emails and load them into the brand's sender as drafts.
Assemble the upload kit.

The refund line appears on the sales page, checkout and receipt.

stages.title: Publish it: open sales and make one real test purchase
stages.what: Claude switches the course from draft to published and the checkout to live. The owner makes one real purchase with his own card, checks he gets in on his phone, then Claude refunds it.
stages.why: Status truth: nothing is live until a real payment grants real access. A real test purchase is the only way to see the receipt, the sign-in email, the order bump and the mission screens exactly as a buyer does.

choices.question: Make one real $27 purchase now, refunded right after?

decided.reason: His spend and status-truth rules.

decided.value: Receipt email arrives, sign-in code works, mission 1 opens, answers save, order bump line is on the receipt, deliverable downloads
decided.reason: His own-site delivery method test.

stages.title: Register the course, launch, and check at 30 days
stages.what: Claude records the live course in HQ, makes the launch pack, and at day 30 reads buyers, completions, refunds and reviews, then recommends feed, fix or kill.
stages.why: His standard says every product reports back. Completion and refunds tell whether the course delivers; reviews unlock the higher-priced rungs.

decided.value: One teach piece showing mission 1's result, one offer piece, a course link on the brand site, the free lead magnet pointing to it, and the email to the list
decided.reason: His launch pack and the outcome-first content method he filed November 24, 2026.

decided.value: Visitors, buyers, finished courses, revenue after refunds
decided.reason: His course engine plan.

decided.value: At least one sale and at least half of buyers finishing mission 1 in 30 days; refunds under 10 percent
decided.reason: Estimate: low-ticket refund rates are commonly quoted at 8 to 15 percent without a stated dataset; Teachable treats under 10 percent as good standing.

work: Add the product_listings row with the live URL and register each mission as a content source.
Make the launch pack inside the brand's mix limits.
At day 30 log revenue in channel_revenue with the Stripe report as evidence and write the feed, fix or kill note.
When 10 reviews exist, flag the brand's next rung as ready.

ai_question.how_to_answer: No host he uses asks an AI question for a course on his own site. Say it plainly anyway: one line on the sales page and the welcome screen that the lessons are produced with AI voice and visuals from the author's own method. If the course is ever listed on Udemy, its description must state whether AI was used, and fully AI-generated courses with minimal instructor input are refused there.
